name: Neoconservatism
summary: Neoconservatism is an American variant of conservatism that arose in the 1970s among former liberals and anti-communists. It accepts a reduced but real welfare state and a qualified market economy built on growth, treats culture and religion as political concerns, and favours an assertive foreign policy that uses American power and promotes democracy abroad while distrusting world government.
scope: The American neoconservative persuasion as Britannica (Ball and Dagger) and Irving Kristol define it, from the 1970s (Kristol, Podhoretz, Glazer, Bell, Moynihan, Kirkpatrick) through the Bush-era foreign policy. It uses Kristol's own accounts, Kirkpatrick's essay that Britannica names as the neoconservative case, and Podhoretz's writing; it excludes think-tank platforms such as PNAC and non-American uses of the term.

notes: Evidence is all words: neoconservatism has no regime or party record. Searched: Kristol's essays (growth, welfare, culture, religion, foreign policy), Britannica, Kirkpatrick and Podhoretz. PNAC material was left out as an organisational platform. Britannica's own copy was read through the Wayback Machine because the site refuses scripted access.
